Lithuania is among the few countries backing the toughest possible sanctions against Russia, with ambitions ranging from closing European borders to Russian soldiers to banning the transport of Russian liquefied natural gas. But Lithuaniaâs ambassador to the EU says Europe is growing tired of punishing the Kremlin. âThe argument heard most often is that sanctions should not harm European countries and their economies compared with Russia,â says Lithuaniaâs ambassador to the EU, Nerijus AleksiejÅ«nas. As a result, restrictions on Russiaâs fishing sector have already been dropped from the sanctions package, while Bulgaria is vetoing sanctions against Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill. France, Italy and Spain are the main opponents of a ban on Russian soldiers entering Europe. They issued the most visas to Russian citizens last year. A compromise appears likely, with the decision postponed until the autumn and handed over to the European Commission, where no member state will be able to veto it. âThe best way to solve this problem is through changes to the visa code, where all the rules are set out,â says AleksiejÅ«nas. The European Commissionâs proposal to ban EU countries from transporting Russian gas and selling tankers to Russia has caused the most controversy. Greece, which manufactures specialised liquefied natural gas tankers, opposes the move. The European Commission bulding in Brussels | AP âThose ice-class vessels capable of transporting Russian liquefied natural gas are specifically designed for the Arctic, and no other country or company apart from Russia is carrying out projects in the Arctic,â says Petras Katinas, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI). Having failed to persuade Athens, the EU is considering allowing an exemption. Greece not only supplies tankers to Russia but also transports Russian gas, worth â¬2bn last year. âThe Greeks are the biggest service providers for Russian LNG,â Katinas says. The gas storage facilities that were depleted during the unusually cold winter are also causing problems. As a result, Russian gas is in demand. This year, imports from Russia were almost a fifth higher than last year, with the EU paying Russia nearly â¬6bn for it. However, imports of Russian gas will be banned from next year. âMore gas is being bought ahead of the ban â we saw the same thing before the previous ban,â Katinas says. There is also debate over the price cap on Russian oil. Lithuaniaâs aim is to keep it frozen at $44 a barrel. If it were recalculated, it would rise to $60, as the EUâs current limit is set at 15% below the market price. Greece, Malta and Cyprus, however, do not want the price cap to remain frozen. âThe signal being sent is that they are backing away from their own sanctions,â Katinas says. Lithuanian diplomats say that despite the disagreements, there are also areas of consensus. âThe aim is to restrict Russiaâs financial market, its access to capital and its access to alternative sources of financing such as cryptocurrencies. Well, there is much more in the package,â AleksiejÅ«nas says. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. Thanks for subscribing! https://www.dw.com/en/zambia-mundubile-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J6zU Opposition leader Brian Mundubile plans to challenge Tuesday's presidential election result [FILE: August 13] Image: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP Advertisement Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile said on Wednesday that he plans to challenge the results of this month's presidential election result in court. Zambia's electoral commission declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema the winner of the election on Tuesday, giving him a second five-year term. He has been in power since 2021. The election was marred by accusations of interference and by arrests of opposition figures . Mundubile heads the opposition NRPUP party that governed Zambia before Hichilema took power in 2021 Image: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP What did Mundubile say about his push to challenge the election result? While announcing his intention to legally challenge the result, Mundubile pointed to irregularities and other issues with the election. "Our campaign ​has documented serious irregularities, inconsistencies and circumstances ​surrounding the conduct, counting, transmission and declaration of results", Mundubile said in a statement issued from an undisclosed location. The politician had earlier said he was under protection due to threats. Mundubile received 38% of the vote on Tuesday, while Hichilema took 60%, according to the electoral commission. While the vote itself was largely peaceful, some 11 people — including leading figures in the opposition — were arrested on the night of the election. The government said that the arrests were part of a raid against "militia activity.” Mundubile's National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) said that shots were fired during the raid of the opposition figure's home. The party also denied any ties to militias. Vote counting was also suspended for multiple hours on Friday after the electoral commission reported attacks against polling officials and theft of some ballots. UN rights chief calls for Zambia to halt arrests, EU mission notes irregularity The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, said he was concerned by reports of arrests of opposition members. In a statement, he urged authorities "to stop arresting people arbitrarily and to uphold fully the due process rights of all those detained." Meanwhile, an electoral observer mission for the European Union raised concerns around transparency. "Observers reported extended breaks during the results tabulation process in almost half of observations, as the returning officers seemed to wait and receive instructions from... headquarters before announcing results," the mission said. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-10/n.text: Explore the ABC Literary giants Joseph Conrad and John Galsworthy owed their friendship to Port Adelaide D By Daniel Keane Topic: English Literature Posted Sat 10 Oct 2026 at 5:30am Sat 10 Oct 2026 at 5:30am Sat 10 Oct 2026 at 5:30am Acclaimed authors Joseph Conrad and John Galsworthy met aboard the clipper ship Torrens in 1893. ( Wikimedia Commons/State Library of South Australia PRG 1373/2/26 ) abc.net.au/news/nobel-winner-john-galsworthy-met-joseph-conrad-at-port-adelaide/107241272 Link copied Share Share article The oceans of the world do not allow us to retrace our steps, for the simple reason that the nature of waves is not conducive to the creation of footprints. But that doesn't mean treasure can't be pursued on the high seas of history. Indeed, it's on those waters that the scholarly wayfarer encounters strange flotsam, sometimes in the form of other human beings. When a young English law graduate met a Polish sailor aboard the clipper ship "Torrens" at Port Adelaide in 1893, neither could have realised they were participating in a moment that would fascinate future generations. But the lawyer was nevertheless prompted to write of the sailor: " He is a man of travel and experience in many parts of the world, and has a fund of yarns on which I draw freely. He has been right up the Congo and all around Malacca and Borneo and other out of the way parts. " The most arresting clue in that description is the word "Congo". The portrait is of Józef Korzeniowski, better known to subsequent generations of readers as Joseph Conrad. The novelist's name is now associated with a series of masterpieces, including Heart of Darkness. A contested work, it has long since occupied an exalted place in the post-colonial canon as an indictment of European brutality in Africa, and was the inspiration for the film Apocalypse Now. Heart of Darkness was the inspiration for Apocalypse Now. ( AFP/Zoetrope Films ) Conrad's portraitist and fellow seafarer was John Galsworthy — a man who would attain an equal literary eminence. In 1932, he was honoured with the Nobel Prize, which was awarded to him largely in recognition of his social saga about a typically myopic upper-middle-class Edwardian family (the wryly named Forsytes) whose members are riven by conflicting senses of duty. The meeting of the two budding authors on the Torrens was purely serendipitous, but its ripples spread across the lives and works of both men, and continue to reach us today. Much has changed since the Torrens docked in 1893, but the maritime atmosphere remains. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Paths to, and from, a meeting In 1893, neither Conrad nor Galsworthy was a published novelist, let alone a public figure, and the paths by which they converged on Port Adelaide were as dissimilar as they were remarkable. Conrad was the more worldly man. Born in 1857 into minor nobility in what is now Ukraine, he was the son of an insurgent opposed to Russian rule over Poland. A newspaper article from 1941 on the friendship between John Galsworthy and Joseph Conrad. ( Trove: The Advertiser ) After resolving while still a child to become a sailor, Conrad voyaged the world and made several journeys to Australia, collecting material for stories along the way. The Oxford-educated Galsworthy, on the other hand, was sent to sea by his father in order to hone skills in maritime law. He also hoped to cross paths with Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson, who had settled in Samoa. Instead, he found Conrad. "In that meeting commenced one of the most loyal of personal and literary friendships, which grew deeper and stronger throughout all the subsequent years," The Age newspaper later reported. The clipper ship "Torrens" docked at Port Adelaide. ( State Library of South Australia B 11871 ) The pair spent weeks aboard the Torrens before Galsworthy disembarked in South Africa. Conrad, who was already at work on his first novel, was perhaps less liable to literary influence than was the impressionable Galsworthy. In a late essay that was also an obituary to his old friend, the Englishman reflected on the times he stayed with Conrad and his wife Jessie, and on the impact Conrad had on his own career. "[Conrad] was indefatigably good to me while my own puppy's eyes were opening to literature, and I was still in the early stages of that struggle with his craft which a writer worth his salt never quite abandons," Galsworthy wrote. A portrait of John Galsworthy from 1909. ( National Portrait Gallery/Creative Commons ) Further light is shed by Elsie Belle Champion, a Melbourne booklover who both visited and corresponded with Galsworthy. Newspaper reports from the 1930s attribute to her the following remarks: "Galsworthy told me that he first thought about writing after having met Joseph Conrad in Adelaide. They had many talks on literature on the ship's bridge at night." Ashes to ashes, waves to waves Neither Galsworthy nor Conrad reached especially old age — Galsworthy died at 65 and Conrad at 66 — but each, in a sense, achieved a tragic longevity. Loading... Both came from backgrounds that suited them for leisure and comfort, but both lived into a time in which it was increasingly impossible to ignore the plain fact of human misery, or to insulate oneself from the impulse to do something about it. They were not temperamentally inclined to what is today called "activism" — which, in any case, is the wrong word for the way in which both responded to the iniquities of the time. European civilisation had produced things (art, culture and modes of living and thinking) they could not help but value, and its greatest gift to them was a kind of urbane conscience. But it was that exact same conscience that compelled these two men to attack at the base some of the unconscionable foundations upon which their own privilege rested. A memorial service was held for Galsworthy at Westminster Abbey, following his death in 1933. ( Reuters: Clodagh Kilcoyne ) They would perhaps not have wished it thus, but they are best remembered by us as pallbearers of empire. "We had been celebrating not only the departure of a noble character and a great writer, but the obituary of an age," journalist Henry Nevinson wrote after the public memorial service for Galsworthy, at Westminster Abbey in 1933. It was an age, Nevinson added, that "was crumbling into the ashes". Galsworthy had sung the swan song of a social class that prided itself on rectitude but that achieved decorum through a great deceit. It was Conrad who traced this deceit to its source. In Heart of Darkness, he savaged the savagery then being inflicted on those deemed "savages". After his death in 1924, Conrad was laid to rest in the cathedral city of Canterbury. A ferry sails across the English Channel towards Dover on the Kent coast, not far from Conrad's resting place in Canterbury. ( Reuters:Toby Melville ) Scottish author Robert Cunninghame Graham accompanied him on his final voyage, from church to burial ground, and penned a poignant reminiscence of the moments that followed the sinking of Conrad's coffin into the soil. "And so we left him with his sails all duly furled … and with the anchor holding truly in the kind Kentish earth," Graham wrote. " The gulls will bring him tidings as they fly past above his grave, with their wild voices, if he should weary for the sea. Danemarca va acorda Ucrainei un nou pachet de asistență militară în valoare de 643 de milioane de euro, a anunțat marți guvernul de la Copenhaga, cu ocazia vizitei președintelui Volodimir Zelenski, scrie Mediafax . Reuniunea cu liderii statelor nordice are loc în aceeași zi în care Ucraina și Rusia au început negocieri directe, mediate de Statele Unite, la Abu Dhabi. Noul pachet de sprijin militar anunțat de autoritățile daneze se ridică la 4,8 miliarde de coroane, echivalentul a aproximativ 643 de milioane de euro, potrivit Euronews. Ministrul danez de Externe, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, a precizat că Danemarca va aloca separat 150 de milioane de coroane, aproximativ 20 de milioane de euro, pentru susținerea sectorului energetic ucrainean. Anunțul vine pe fondul continuării atacurilor rusești asupra infrastructurii civile și energetice din Ucraina, în apropierea sezonului rece. Președintele ucrainean Volodimir Zelenski a sosit marți la Copenhaga pentru discuții privind securitatea regională și continuarea sprijinului acordat Kievului. Premierul danez Mette Frederiksen a salutat vizita liderului ucrainean și a reafirmat susținerea țării sale pentru Ucraina. „Sunt mândră să îi primesc în Danemarca pe președintele Zelenski și pe liderii nordici. Lupta ucrainenilor pentru o Ucraină liberă și o Europă liberă continuă”, a transmis Frederiksen. La reuniunea de la Copenhaga erau așteptați și premierul Suediei, Ulf Kristersson, premierul Norvegiei, Jonas Gahr Støre, și premierul Finlandei, Petteri Orpo. Întâlnirea are loc într-un moment important pentru eforturile diplomatice de încheiere a războiului, în condițiile în care delegațiile Ucrainei și Rusiei au început marți discuții directe la Abu Dhabi, cu medierea Statelor Unite. Țările nordice se numără printre principalii susținători europeni ai Ucrainei, atât prin asistență militară, cât și prin sprijin financiar și diplomatic. Mette Frederiksen a subliniat că atacurile asupra populației civile și a infrastructurii esențiale continuă, în ciuda eforturilor diplomatice. Premierul danez a atras atenția că, la aproape cinci ani de la declanșarea invaziei rusești la scară largă, sunt vizate în continuare centre de ajutor umanitar și instalații de alimentare cu apă și căldură. Reuniunea are loc și pe fondul unor divergențe diplomatice între statele nordice privind contactele directe cu Moscova. La sfârșitul lunii octombrie, Zelenski a vizitat Oslo, unde s-a întâlnit cu emisari americani. Ulterior, premierul norvegian Jonas Gahr Støre și președintele finlandez Alexander Stubb au purtat o convorbire telefonică de aproximativ 90 de minute cu Vladimir Putin. Stubb a descris discuția drept una sinceră și substanțială, însă premierul danez a criticat inițiativa, susținând că aceasta nu fusese coordonată cu celelalte state nordice. Vizita președintelui ucrainean a determinat consolidarea măsurilor de securitate în capitala daneză. În zona sediului premierului danez a fost desfășurat un dispozitiv important de poliție, iar autoritățile au anunțat restricții suplimentare pentru zilele următoare. Poliția din Copenhaga a precizat că zborurile dronelor deasupra capitalei vor fi interzise până pe 12 noiembrie. Noul angajament financiar al Danemarcei confirmă continuarea sprijinului militar pentru Ucraina, în paralel cu negocierile diplomatice care urmăresc identificarea unei soluții pentru încetarea războiului.
